facts.claim: "The Sad Ballad of Danny Boy" is track 14 on Floater's album Glyph, runs 3:17, and was released in 1995 on Elemental Records, Inc.
Robert Wynia is credited as the songwriter of "The Sad Ballad of Danny Boy".

Glyph was produced by Floater. Credits list Rob Wynia on bass, vocals, percussion, acoustic guitar and synthesizer, Pete Cornett on drums and percussion, and Dave Amador on guitar. Backing vocals are by Julie Breighaupt and Princess Angela. Drew Canulette mixed the album and Kevin Nettleingham mastered it.
Glyph was recorded by Michael Wilson at Studio Apocalypse in Eugene, Oregon, and by Drew Canulette at Musicraft in Wilsonville, Oregon.
"The Sad Ballad of Danny Boy" was first recorded on the Sink demo tape, before the Sink album came out. Wikipedia's Glyph article says the song also got national radio play.
The song is a ballad about a man named Danny Boy who lives for drinking at the pub. His family begs him to come home earlier.
Glyph was a followup to Sink and produced a major local hit with "The Sad Ballad of Danny Boy".

Floater was formed in 1993 in Eugene, Oregon, by singer/bassist Robert Wynia and drummer Peter Cornett, who had previously played together in Henry's Child. They added guitarist David Amador, recorded a six-song demo, and released their debut LP Sink on Elemental in 1994.

Floater toured the country for two years in support of Glyph. The band received preliminary Grammy nominations from NARAS: Best Rock Performance for Sink in 1995 and Best Alternative Performance for Glyph in 1996.

Floater turned down offers from Capitol Records and Zoo Records and stayed with Elemental Records to keep creative control. After Sink, Wynia started his own label, Typhon Records, whose imprint appears alongside Elemental's from Glyph through The Great Release.

research.lineage: Floater began as a predominantly metal/hard rock band from the Eugene, Oregon scene, with bass-driven songs, some influence from Primus and hard rock, and a handful of acoustic songs on the early albums.

draft:
The chorus of **The Sad Ballad of Danny Boy** is a quotation inside a quotation. The family steps in first, begging "Oh Danny, won't you go home earlier tonight?", and then repeats back what he says when he finally does come home. So the man's own words reach us through the people afraid of him: "With you the violence just comes so easily." In his mouth, the violence belongs to them. They made him do it. "You never learn I have to teach you constantly" is the self-justification of someone who has turned beating into parenting, and the song lets that logic sit there, ugly and calm.

Robert Wynia wrote it, and the verses give Danny a breezy, almost likable voice. He introduces himself like a barroom regular, buys "a pint or three," and when the pub closes he heads to the market, reasoning that "the sun is always up somewhere." It's the drinker's oldest loophole, delivered with a grin. The pain is in the small swaps between choruses. First it's "your daughter doesn't know you," then "your son." Two children, the same stranger for a father. Then "hush now," repeated until it stops sounding like a threat and starts sounding like a lullaby: "Sleep floating child." Whether that's the kids learning to go quiet or the song putting them to bed out of mercy, it never says.

Calling it a ballad is the first trick. Floater play it fast and hard. A distorted guitar from Dave Amador works a riff over a simple, pushing bass line, and Pete Cornett's drums drive it with a snare that sits up front. Wynia's voice is raw and strained, forceful, with no harmonies to soften it. The production is unpolished, which suits a song that won't dress Danny up. This is the Eugene, Oregon band that came out of metal and hard rock, with Primus somewhere in the bloodstream, and here that heaviness serves a domestic story, not a show of muscle.

The song goes back to the Sink demo tape, before the band's 1994 debut, and turned up on 1995's *Glyph*, recorded between Studio Apocalypse in Eugene and Musicraft in Wilsonville. It became a major local hit and got national radio play, which is a little startling given what it's about. Maybe the chorus is just loud enough to shout along to before you notice what you're shouting.

What sticks is that the loudest, catchiest part of the song is a family repeating their abuser's excuses back to him, and you end up singing them too.
